sections.title: Global Equities
sections.content:
September delivered a deeply bifurcated global equity tape. While AI-linked technology names carried the Nasdaq Composite to a monthly gain of **+1.9%**, the broader market told a starkly different story: the S&P 500 slipped **-0.5%** and the Dow Jones Industrial Average plunged **-4.3%**, as surging Treasury yields, resurgent energy prices, and a hawkish Federal Reserve reset punished rate-sensitive and cyclical sectors alike.

European bourses bore the brunt of the global yield surge and oil shock, with the DAX falling **-4.0%**, the CAC 40 declining **-4.4%**, and the FTSE 100 shedding **-2.0%**. Asia-Pacific markets were similarly challenged: Japan navigated a Bank of Japan rate hike to **1.25%** with characteristic volatility, while the Hang Seng remained under pressure from global risk-off dynamics and persistent Chinese macro headwinds.

Beneath headline indices, breadth deteriorated to alarming levels. Approximately **83%** of S&P 500 members traded more than **10%** below their 52-week highs by month-end, and roughly **42%** were down more than **20%**—a divergence emblematic of a market powered by a narrow cohort of mega-cap AI beneficiaries.

sections.title: Your Must-Know Market Themes
sections.content: Four key themes that shaped markets this month:
themes:
Fed Resumes Tightening Cycle -- The Federal Reserve's September 16 decision to raise the federal funds target range by **25 basis points** to **3.75%–4.00%**—its first hike since 2023—marked a pivotal policy shift that reverberated across every asset class. The unanimous **12-0** vote reflected Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's conviction that inflation remained durably above the **2%** target, compounded by oil-supply risks arising from Middle East geopolitical tension. Treasury markets had already pre-positioned aggressively; the 10-year yield surged toward multi-decade highs ahead of and following the decision.

The updated dot plot now points to one additional **25 bp** hike at the December 2026 meeting, followed by a prolonged hold, with rate cuts not projected until 2028—a timeline materially more hawkish than market expectations at the start of the year. Equity markets responded along familiar fault lines: rate-sensitive sectors including real estate, utilities, and small caps sold off materially, while technology companies with fortress balance sheets and AI-driven earnings upgrades proved comparatively resilient. The September hike crystallised the central question for Q4: whether AI-economy winners can sustain their premium valuations in a durably higher-for-longer rate environment.

Global Bond Market Rout -- September 2026 delivered one of the most severe global sovereign bond sell-offs in decades. The US 10-year Treasury yield breached **5%** for the first time since 2007, ultimately settling near **5.29%** at month-end—a rise of roughly **50 basis points** over the month (approx., verify before merging)—while the 30-year bond yield scaled above **5.6%**, its highest level since 2002. The sell-off was multi-causal: the Fed's rate hike, Brent crude trading above **$100/bbl**, mounting fiscal deficit concerns, and heavy AI-related infrastructure debt issuance all contributed to a relentless supply-demand imbalance at the long end.

Critically, the move was driven by surging real yields rather than inflation breakeven rates, with TIPS yields rising sharply as investors demanded higher compensation for fiscal sustainability risk and AI-related bond supply. The global spillover was pronounced: UK gilts, German Bunds, French OATs, and Japanese government bonds all sold off in sympathy, with JGB yields reaching their highest level since 1996. Investment-grade and high-yield credit spreads widened materially, raising the cost of capital for corporates globally and intensifying the debate about whether the bond market had completed its repricing or was in the early stages of a structural regime shift.

Oil Surge and Middle East Risk Premium -- Brent crude rallied more than **10%** during September, trading above **$100 per barrel** for much of the month before settling near **$98/bbl** at month-end—the first sustained triple-digit print in several years. The primary catalyst was escalating US-Iran geopolitical tension, which injected a pronounced risk premium into global energy markets and raised concrete fears of Strait of Hormuz supply disruption. OPEC+ supply discipline and stronger-than-expected US demand data provided secondary support, limiting the scope for any price reversal.

Energy's gain came at a material cost to the broader economy and equity markets. Higher oil prices functioned as an implicit consumer tax and a margin headwind for energy-intensive industries, contributing directly to the sharp underperformance of cyclicals and consumer discretionary names. The oil rally also served as a significant multiplier on inflationary pressures, reinforcing the Fed's decision to resume tightening and accelerating the bond sell-off. Elsewhere in commodities, gold fell more than **6%** to close near **$4,187/oz** as the dollar surged and real yields rose sharply—a textbook adverse read-through for non-yielding precious metals.

AI CapEx Bifurcation Deepens -- September confirmed the market's extreme concentration in a narrow cohort of mega-cap AI beneficiaries. The Nasdaq Composite gained **+1.9%** even as the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell **-4.3%**—a **630 basis-point** monthly spread illustrating the degree to which AI-linked technology capital flows have decoupled from the broader equity market. Cloud hyperscalers, semiconductor designers, and AI infrastructure companies continued to attract investment despite rising financing costs, buoyed by earnings revisions that repeatedly outpaced elevated consensus expectations.

The structural irony of the month was that heavy AI-related debt issuance—as tech giants tapped credit markets at scale to fund data centre and compute buildouts—was itself identified as a direct contributor to upward pressure on long-end Treasury yields. This created a self-reinforcing dynamic: AI CapEx growth drove equity leadership for the AI cohort while simultaneously widening the cost of capital for all other borrowers. With breadth at cycle lows, approximately **83%** of S&P 500 members in correction or worse, and AI-cohort valuations approaching historical extremes, the sustainability of this bifurcation became the central strategic debate heading into Q4 2026.

sections.title: US Equities
sections.content:
September's US equity outcome was almost entirely a function of AI ecosystem proximity. The Nasdaq Composite rose **+1.9%** to close at **26,861**, driven by mega-cap technology and AI-infrastructure names that absorbed higher discount rates through persistent earnings upgrades. By contrast, the S&P 500 slipped **-0.5%** to **7,652** and the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell **-4.3%** to **50,906**, as rate-sensitive sectors—financials, real estate, utilities, and industrials—bore the full brunt of a **50+ basis-point** yield re-rating across the Treasury curve (approx., verify before merging).

The Fed's **25 bp** hike to **3.75%–4.00%** on September 16 was the central catalyst, compounding a month-long rise in yields that repriced virtually every equity sector outside the narrow AI cohort. Consumer confidence surveys softened in response to both higher borrowing costs and elevated gasoline prices tied to a Brent crude print above **$100/bbl**. Small and mid-cap indices registered losses materially in excess of large-cap benchmarks, consistent with their greater sensitivity to floating-rate debt servicing costs and tighter financial conditions.

Breadth deterioration was the defining sub-surface development: with approximately **83%** of S&P 500 members trading more than **10%** below their 52-week highs and roughly **42%** down more than **20%**, the index's near-flat performance masked a market in which the vast majority of constituents were in correction or bear-market territory. Q3 earnings season, launching in early October, is expected to sharpen the debate over whether AI-driven earnings leadership can sustainably offset a deteriorating macro backdrop.

sections.title: European Equities
sections.content:
European equity markets endured a challenging September, with all major benchmarks posting material declines as the twin headwinds of surging sovereign yields and elevated energy costs compressed valuations. The DAX fell **-4.0%** to close at **25,199**, the CAC 40 declined **-4.4%** to **7,965**, and the FTSE 100 shed **-2.0%** to **10,606**—the FTSE's comparative outperformance attributable to its significant energy and commodity sector weighting, which provided a partial offset as Brent crude traded above **$100/bbl**.

The global bond sell-off hit European government paper hard in sympathy with US Treasuries, raising discount rates and compressing price-to-earnings multiples across the continent. The European Central Bank faces an acute policy dilemma: with energy prices reigniting inflation just as activity data points to slowing momentum, markets remain divided on the pace and terminal level of any further tightening. AI-linked CapEx themes that have been the primary driver of US equity outperformance have far fewer direct analogues in European index compositions, leaving continental bourses more exposed to the macro headwinds.

Germany's industrial base remained under particular pressure, with the DAX's sharp underperformance reflecting persistent structural concerns about energy-intensive manufacturing competitiveness, stagnant domestic demand, and the relative absence of high-multiple technology representation. The CAC 40's outsized decline was compounded by weakness in luxury goods and consumer-facing names, where softening Chinese demand added a second leg of pressure atop the domestic yield shock.

sections.title: APAC Equities
sections.content:
Asia-Pacific markets presented a nuanced picture in September, with Japan's BOJ policy action driving distinctive dynamics. The Bank of Japan raised its policy rate by **25 basis points** to **1.25%**—the highest level since 1995—on September 18, and in a notable departure from the conventional playbook, the Nikkei 225 rose on the day as markets interpreted the hike as a signal of confidence in Japan's economic recovery rather than a tightening shock. The Nikkei 225 closed September at approximately **66,754** (approx., verify before merging), recovering sharply from mid-month lows near **63,655** following the BOJ announcement.

The Hang Seng closed September at approximately **24,613** (approx., verify before merging), remaining under pressure from a combination of global risk-off sentiment, elevated US yields raising the opportunity cost for emerging market equities, and continued concerns about Chinese property sector stabilisation. The Shanghai Composite remained broadly weak through September, though precise end-of-month levels were not confirmed across available sources.

Japan's macroeconomic backdrop provided positive signals late in the month: September export growth came in at **+16.7%** year-over-year, extending a 13-month streak of expansion. JGB yields rose to their highest level since 1996, reflecting both the BOJ's policy normalisation and global fixed income contagion from the US Treasury sell-off—a dynamic that will test the central bank's conviction at its October 29–30 meeting, where consensus currently expects a hold before a potential December move.

sections.title: Foreign Exchange
sections.content:
The US dollar reasserted broad dominance in September. The DXY dollar index gained approximately **+2.4%** as the Fed's rate hike, surging real Treasury yields, and risk-off portfolio flows coalesced into a powerful bid for the greenback. EUR/USD fell **-2.25%** to close at **1.1400**, with the euro pressured by policy divergence between a Fed resuming tightening and a more conflicted ECB, compounded by higher European energy import costs from the oil rally. GBP/USD declined **-1.90%** to **1.3300**, with sterling finding only partial support from the Bank of England's own hawkish guidance.

The yen's September trajectory was the notable exception to broad dollar strength. USD/JPY closed the month at approximately **157.00**, recording a monthly change of approximately **-1.7%** (approx., verify before merging; sign convention varied across sources). The BOJ's rate hike to **1.25%** on September 18 provided the yen with fundamental support at a time when the US-Japan rate differential, while still wide, was narrowing at the margin. Intraday price action on BOJ day was atypical—the yen initially weakened before the broader monthly trend of yen appreciation reasserted.

Emerging market currencies faced headwinds from dollar strength and higher US real yields, with commodity-linked currencies receiving only partial offset from the energy and oil rally. The DXY's break above key technical resistance levels mid-month prompted a further round of risk reduction in FX carry trades, amplifying directional moves across both G10 and EM pairs.

sections.title: Commodities
sections.content:
Energy dominated the commodities complex in September. Brent crude surged more than **10%** during the month, trading above **$100 per barrel** for an extended period and settling near **$98/bbl** at month-end—the first sustained foray into triple-digit territory in several years. WTI crude tracked closely, with the Brent-WTI differential maintained near historical norms. The rally's primary catalyst was geopolitical: escalating US-Iran tensions injected a pronounced risk premium reflecting fears of Strait of Hormuz supply disruption, with OPEC+ supply discipline and resilient US demand providing secondary support.

Gold reversed course sharply after a strong run earlier in the year. The precious metal fell more than **6%** to close near **$4,187/oz**, as surging real Treasury yields raised the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding assets and the dollar's broad rally removed a structural support pillar. The combination of rising real rates and a strengthening greenback represents the classic adverse macro configuration for gold, and the speed of the sell-off reflected the scale of position unwinding from prior highs.

Copper traded in a range of approximately **$6.60–$6.80 per lb** (approx., verify before merging), with COMEX month-end closes near **$6.65/lb**, broadly supported by the IMF's monthly series showing September prices around **$14,473/metric ton**. The industrial metal navigated mixed signals: AI data centre construction and energy transition infrastructure provided demand tailwinds, while softening Chinese industrial activity and the global risk-off backdrop capped upside. Agricultural commodities and broader base metals were largely range-bound amid the macro noise.

sections.title: Fixed Income
sections.content:
September was a landmark month for fixed income markets. The US 10-year Treasury yield breached **5%** for the first time since 2007, ultimately settling at approximately **5.29%** on September 30—a rise of roughly **50 basis points** over the month (approx., verify before merging). The 30-year bond yield scaled above **5.6%**, its highest level since 2002, while the 2-year note closed near **4.89–4.93%**, producing a positively sloped yield curve with a term spread of approximately **35–40 basis points** between the 2-year and 10-year.

The sell-off was driven principally by surging real yields rather than inflation breakeven rates—underscoring that investors were demanding higher compensation for fiscal sustainability risk and AI-related bond supply rather than pricing incremental inflation. The Fed's **25 bp** hike to **3.75%–4.00%** added institutional confirmation to what markets had pre-positioned for, while the dot plot's terminal rate projection of **4.10%** for 2026 validated the aggressive repricing. Investment-grade credit spreads widened on the move, and high-yield spreads widened more materially, though both remained below levels associated with historical distress episodes.

Global spillovers were substantial. UK gilts, German Bunds, and French OATs sold off in sympathy, driven by shared inflation, fiscal deficit, and AI-debt-supply themes. JGB yields reached their highest level since 1996, testing the Bank of Japan's tolerance for fixed income market volatility concurrent with its own rate normalisation. The magnitude and velocity of the global yield surge prompted serious debate among strategists about whether September's bond market repricing represented a durable structural shift toward a higher-rate equilibrium—or a technically-extended overshoot that would revert as macro data inevitably cooled heading into Q4.
